lede: A third is $0.333\ldots$, going on for ever, and it is still an ordinary fraction. Every recurring decimal is. A short method finds exactly which fraction, with one subtraction that makes the endless tail disappear.
can: Read the dot notation and say which digits repeat.
Choose the multipliers from the digits before and inside the block.
Subtract, clear any decimal, and simplify the fraction.

text: 1. Two numbers with the same tail

md: You cannot write $0.\dot{4}$ out in full, and rounding it throws the exactness away. The way round is to make a second number with exactly the same endless tail, then subtract. Call the decimal $x$. Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place left, and because every digit is a 4, the tail of $10x$ is the tail of $x$.

alt: Two rows of working lined up at the decimal point: x = 0.4444444… and 10x = 4.4444444…, with the digits after the point shaded to show they are identical. Under a rule, 9x = 4, so x = 4/9.

title: Why the tails cancel
md: Both lines carry the same digits for ever after the point, so taking one from the other cancels every one of them. Nothing is rounded, which is why the fraction is exact, not an approximation.

stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{4}$ to a fraction.

steps.decision: Naming the decimal lets you make a second copy of it. This line is the first thing the scheme looks for.
One digit repeats, so multiply by 10: the point moves one place and the tails line up.
Subtract. Every 4 after the point cancels, and whole numbers are left on both sides.
Divide by 9. It is already in its lowest terms.

md: In $0.\dot{3}\dot{6}$ the dots mark the first and last digits of the block, so 36 repeats: $0.363636\ldots$ Multiplying by 10 would shift it half a block, and the tails would not match. Use one power of ten for each digit in the block: 100 for two digits, 1000 for three. Then the subtraction leaves 99 or 999 on the left.

text: 3. When a digit does not repeat

md: In $0.7\dot{2}$ the dot sits over the 2 only, so the 7 happens once and never again. One multiplication cannot line up both. So do two: multiply by 10 to push the 7 past the point, then by 100 to move one block further. Those two lines share a tail; subtract them.

There is a shorter route, and CCEA's schemes use it: subtract $x$ from $10x$ straight away. The right-hand side then ends, as $9x = 6.5$ does. A decimal that ends is not an error; multiply top and bottom by 10.

stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.7\dot{2}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.decision: Only the 2 carries a dot, so the 7 is outside the block. That decision sets everything else.
Multiply by 10 to push the 7 past the point. From here on everything after the point repeats.
One block further: this line and the last now share a tail.
Subtract the pair with matching tails, divide, and simplify by 5.
The same fraction by the other route. A right-hand side that ends is fine: multiply top and bottom by 10.

prompt: Change $0.4\dot{6}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
explain: Steps 2 to 4 of See it: $10x = 4.666\ldots$ and $100x = 46.666\ldots$, so $90x = 42$ and $x = \dfrac{42}{90} = \dfrac{7}{15}$. Treating both digits as repeating would give $\dfrac{46}{99}$.

explain: Step 5 of See it: the right-hand side ends, so the tails did cancel. $x = \dfrac{3.1}{9}$, and multiplying top and bottom by 10 clears the decimal: $\dfrac{31}{90}$.

twin.prompt: Working on $0.0\dot{4}\dot{5}$, you subtract $x$ from $100x$ and get $99x = 4.5$. What next?
options: Start again: the multiplier must be wrong
twin.explain: 4.5 ends, so the tails did cancel. $\dfrac{4.5}{99} = \dfrac{45}{990}$, which simplifies to $\dfrac{1}{22}$.

optionNotes.option: Start again: the multiplier must be wrong
optionNotes.why: The subtraction left a number that ends, so the tails matched. Only a tail that still goes on would mean the multiplier was wrong.
Rounding changes the value: $\dfrac{5}{99}$ is $0.0505\ldots$, not $0.0454\ldots$

optionNotes.option: Start again: the multiplier must be wrong
optionNotes.why: Only an endless tail left on the right means the lines did not match. A decimal that ends, like 3.1, is expected on this route; CCEA's schemes run $9x = 7.3$.
Rounding throws the exactness away: $\dfrac{3}{9}$ is $0.333\ldots$, not the decimal you started with.

text: 4. A digit before a longer block

md: The two moves combine. Count the digits between the point and the block, $a$, and the digits in the block, $b$. Multiply by $10^{a}$ and by $10^{a+b}$, and subtract those two lines. In $0.1\dot{3}\dot{6}$, $a = 1$ and $b = 2$, so the lines are $10x$ and $1000x$, and the subtraction leaves $990x$.

title: The recipe
md: Let $x$ be the decimal. Multiply by $10^{a}$ and $10^{a+b}$, subtract those two lines, clear any decimal, then simplify. When nothing sits before the block, $a = 0$ and the first line is $x$ itself.

stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.1\dot{3}\dot{6}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.working: Let $x = 0.13636\ldots$: one digit before the block, a block of two.
steps.decision: Read the dots: they sit over the 3 and the 6, so the 1 is outside the block.
$10^{a}$ with $a = 1$ pushes the 1 past the point.
$10^{a+b}$ with $a + b = 3$ moves one whole block further.
Subtract the two lines with matching tails, then simplify: 135 and 990 share 45.

explain: As in See it: $1000x = 218.1818\ldots$ and $10x = 2.1818\ldots$, so $990x = 216$ and $x = \dfrac{216}{990} = \dfrac{12}{55}$. The 990 is the sign that both moves were used.

The easier one, one move. Use a new letter so the two do not get mixed.

text: 6. Why every recurring decimal is a fraction

md: The method never fails on a recurring decimal, and that is the point of it: it proves every recurring decimal is **rational**, one whole number divided by another. A decimal that neither ends nor repeats, like the one for $\sqrt{2}$, never lines up with a copy of itself, and that is what makes it irrational.

title: Not on this specification
md: Infinite-series or limit arguments, and proving that a number is irrational. Deciding whether a given number is rational belongs to the surds statement, M8-NA-01, a separate topic here.

stem: Explain why any recurring decimal can be written as a fraction.

steps.decision: That is the definition of a rational number.

Because a recurring decimal can be rounded to a fraction

answer: Because it always ends with x equal to one whole number divided by another
explain: Steps 3 and 4 of See it: the subtraction always leaves whole numbers once any decimal is cleared, so $x$ is one integer over another. That is what rational means.

optionNotes.option: Because a recurring decimal can be rounded to a fraction
optionNotes.why: Rounding gives a fraction close to the decimal, not equal to it. Rational means exactly one whole number over another.

optionNotes.option: Because every decimal, recurring or not, is rational
optionNotes.why: A decimal that never ends and never repeats, like the one for $\sqrt{2}$, is irrational: without a repeat there is no copy to subtract.

twin.answer: One that never ends and never repeats, such as 0.1010010001…
